bib.title: MathPrompter: Mathematical Reasoning using Large Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: MathPrompter: Mathematical Reasoning using Large Language Models. Shima Imani, Liang Du, Harsh Shrivastava (Microsoft Research). arXiv:2303.05398v1 [cs.CL], 4 Mar 2023. The PDF names no venue and I did not look one up, so I treat it as a preprint. The target note 03-core-techniques.md has no existing mention of "mathprompter" or "imani" (grep returned nothing).

COVERAGE: 23516 of 23516 chars read, in a single pass. That covers the abstract, method, Table 1, Table 2, conclusions, the limitation section and the references. Nothing was skipped. There are no appendices. The paper is 7 pages.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Claim: MathPrompter raises zero-shot-CoT accuracy on MultiArith from 78.7% to 92.5% with a 175B GPT-3 model.
  number: 78.7% -> 92.5%
  setup: MultiArith only. GPT-3 DaVinci completion engine, 175B. Zero-shot, with N~5 repeats and a consensus vote. The Kojima baseline figures are borrowed from Kojima et al. (2022), who used text-davinci-002 (175B). The paper does not say whether MathPrompter used the same GPT-3 version as that baseline, so the comparison may not be like for like.
  quote: "Our technique improves over state-of-the-art on the MultiArith dataset ( 78.7% → 92.5%) evaluated using 175B parameter GPT-based LLM."
  where: p.1, abstract; repeated in Fig. 1 caption and Sec. 3.3.1.
- Claim: The method has four steps. (I) Replace the numbers in the question with variables to make an algebraic template, keeping a key-value mapping. (II) Prompt the LLM for an algebraic expression and for a Python function. (III) Evaluate both with eval() on several random variable assignments and check that they agree. (IV) Repeat about 5 times and take the most frequent answer, then substitute the original values.
  number: N~5 repeats, 2 solution styles
  setup: Described on a single worked example (a restaurant meal-cost question). The "N~5 different variable choices" in the Fig. 1 caption and "repeat steps (II) & (III) for N~5 times" in Sec. 2.1 are two different things, and the paper does not clearly separate them. The caption also says that with no consensus, steps II-IV are repeated.
  quote: "In order to ensure that consensus is reached among various expressions' output, in our experiments, we repeat the steps (II) & (III) for N∼ 5 times and report the most frequent value observed for the answer."
  where: p.3, Sec. 2.1 (IV); Fig. 1 caption, p.2.
- Claim: Prompts used. The algebraic prompt is "Write a mathematical equation and generate the answer format starting with 'Answer ='". The Python prompt is "Write a Python function that returns the answer."
  number: none
  quote: "Algebraic prompt: Write a mathematical equation and generate the answer format starting with ‘Answer =’ Python prompt: Write a Python function that returns the answer."
  where: p.3, Sec. 2.1 (II)
- Claim: The zero-shot MathPrompter result is comparable to few-shot CoT with 8 examples and above zero-shot-CoT plus self-consistency on a 540B model. Table 1 lists the rows below.
  number: Zero-shot 17.7; Zero-shot-CoT 78.7; Zero-shot-CoT (PaLM 540B) 66.1; Zero-shot-CoT + self-consistency (PaLM 540B) 89.0; MathPrompter 92.5; Few-Shot-CoT 2/4/8 samples 84.8/90.5/93.0; Few-Shot 2/8 samples 33.7/33.8
  setup: MultiArith. Rows are 175B unless marked. Baselines are borrowed from Kojima et al. (2022), using the same 8 examples as Wei et al. (2022). The few-shot-CoT row (93.0) beats MathPrompter by 0.5 points. MathPrompter is described as "comparable", not better, than it.
  quote: "Zero-shot-CoT + self consistency (PaLM 540B) 89.0 / Zero-shot-CoT (MathPrompter) 92.5 / ... Few-Shot-CoT (8 samples) 93.0"
  where: p.4, Table 1
- Claim: Zero-shot-CoT (Kojima) has no check on its intermediate steps and gives no confidence. This is the gap the paper says it addresses. Agreement between the algebraic and Python outputs serves as the confidence signal.
  number: none
  quote: "there is no check on the validity of the steps followed by the chain-of-thought prompting and (2) The conﬁdence in the predictions of LLMs are often not provided."
  where: p.1, Sec. 1
- Claim: Authors' qualitative argument, shown on 4 hand-picked examples (Table 2). Consensus across runs avoids one-step errors. Python or algebra uses fewer tokens than long CoT text. Delegating arithmetic to eval() avoids correct reasoning followed by a wrong final computation. These are qualitative observations with no measured numbers.
  number: none
  setup: Table 2, 4 examples. In the first three the CoT answer is wrong and MathPrompter gives 81, 18 and 2. That is 81 correct; 18 correct; 2 wrong (the true answer is 3 trips, so this is the 3rd error case). In the 4th, CoT is correct (54) and MathPrompter is wrong (79).
  quote: "the reasoning steps in Kojima et al. (2022) can be excessively lengthy, but the Pythonic or Algebraic methods can address this by typically requiring fewer tokens."
  where: p.5, Sec. 3.3.2
- Claim: Fail case. Algebraic and Python outputs can agree and both be wrong, so agreement is not a guarantee of correctness. This is the paper's own stated limitation.
  number: none
  setup: Table 2, last row. The Kaleb candy question: both expressions give A*C - B = 79 (the correct answer is 84-30=54, per the CoT column).
  quote: "Both Algebraic and Pythonic expressions have the potential to produce the incorrect results, even if the prompt outputs match each other."
  where: p.6, Sec. 5 Limitation (and p.5-6 Sec. 3.3.2)

LIMITS
- Only one dataset (MultiArith) and one model family (GPT-3 175B). The authors plan to "further evaluate performance on additional datasets". Their work does not show GSM8K or other benchmarks.
- No ablations. There is no single-prompt versus two-prompt comparison, no sweep over N, and no cost or token numbers, although token savings are claimed. The number of runs or seeds is not given.
- The "confidence" claim is not measured. There is no calibration analysis, only the statement that agreement raises confidence.
- Correlated errors can pass the consensus check. This is conceded in the Limitation section. The authors say more prompts would mitigate it, but they do not test that.
- The Sec. 3.2 description of the Brown et al. zero-shot baseline (classifying unseen classes) is garbled and unrelated to prompting. Treat that section with care.
- The tool is limited to problems where the numbers can be abstracted into variables.
- Dated: GPT-3 DaVinci and PaLM numbers from 2022 are far below current model levels. The "SOTA" claims apply only to early 2023. The technique itself (program-aided / tool-offloaded arithmetic plus voting) is the lasting part.
- The code that runs eval() on model output has no sandboxing and the paper does not discuss security.

BUILDS ON
- Kojima et al. (2022), zero-shot-CoT ("Let's think step by step"); this is the baseline and the main starting point.
- Wei et al. (2022), chain-of-thought prompting.
- Wang et al. (2022), self-consistency.
- Brown et al. (2020), GPT-3 and in-context learning.
- Roy & Roth (2016), MultiArith; Koncel-Kedziorski et al. (2016), MAWPS repository.
- Human verification habits are listed as inspiration: compliance with known results, multi-verification, cross-checking and compute verification.

CODE
Worked example, p.3, Sec. 2.1:
Qt: at a restaurant, each adult meal costs A and kids eat free. if a group of B people came in and C were kids, how much would it cost for the group to eat?
Mapping: {A:5, B:15, C:8}
Answer = A *(B-C)
def total_price(A, B, C):
    return A * (B-C)
(The extraction lost the indentation under def. The answers are 35 from both algebraic and Python.)

FIGURES
- Fig. 1 (p.2), MathPrompter flow: the four stages (algebraic template, math-prompts, compute verification with eval(), statistical significance). It is the fastest way to see the pipeline. I did not run the figures script, since the caption text came through in the extraction.
- Table 1 (p.4) and Table 2 (p.5) are tables, covered in the claims above.

PROBLEMS
- The text has ligature artifacts. Code indentation was lost.
- The PDF contains no embedded instructions.
- The venue is not stated in the PDF, so I report it as a preprint.
- Wording of the Table 2 first-row note: "ONE UNNECESSARY STEP ERROR" is the label the authors give the CoT output. I did not verify any Table 2 answers beyond the arithmetic above, and my reading of the 3rd row (Jerry trips) is my own check: the correct answer is 16/8 = 2 trips, so MathPrompter's 2 is right and the CoT answer 3 is wrong. The paper's own label there is "COMMONSENSE MISTAKE" on the CoT side. Please verify before citing that row. Also, in the 2nd row, MathPrompter's answer 18 = 3*(9-3) is right.
- Correction to my row-by-row note above: the CoT outputs are wrong in rows 1-3 and MathPrompter is right in rows 1-3 (81, 18, 2). Only row 4 (Kaleb) is where MathPrompter fails, with 79 against the correct 54, tagged "(COMMONSENSE MISTAKE)".
